items.explanation: The cartoon — presumably satirizing anti-French hysteria and the Alien and Sedition Acts — could most plausibly have appeared during the Quasi-War with France in 1798. That undeclared naval conflict produced the same politics of fear: Federalists warning of French subversion, the Sedition Act jailing critics, foreigners suspected as agents. The earlier episode mirrors the cartoon's themes of panic and repression.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The 1890s depression was economic; it did not produce this cartoon's political themes.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Progressive Era's reform spirit differs from the cartoon's panic-and-repression subject.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Second Great Awakening was a religious revival, not a political panic.
option_explanations.D: Correct. A comparable cartoon could have appeared during the Quasi-War with France in 1798.

items.stem: The declaration's political outlook is most similar to which of the following?
options: (A) Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (1918).
(B) The Bretton Woods agreements (1944) that created the International Monetary Fund.
(C) The New Left's critiques of the Vietnam War in the 1960s.
(D) The Republican Contract with America (1994).
items.explanation: The Global Exchange declaration's outlook — denouncing corporate-dominated globalization, demanding democratic accountability and protections for workers and the environment — echoes the New Left's critiques of the Vietnam War era: suspicion of American power, solidarity with the oppressed, and demands that institutions serve people rather than profits. The Seattle protesters inherited the 1960s left's moral vocabulary.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Wilson's Fourteen Points were a liberal-internationalist war-aims program, not an anti-corporate protest outlook.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Bretton Woods built the postwar economic order the protesters were criticizing.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The declaration's outlook most resembles the New Left's 1960s critiques.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Contract with America was a conservative Republican program — the protesters' opposite.

items.stem: A defining characteristic of the Clinton presidency was his

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov-POTUS}}: official White House photograph, a work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.

options: A. Strict loyalty to traditional Democratic values
B. Pragmatic, centrist policy making
C. A close alliance with party liberals
D. An unprecedented partnership with unions
items.explanation: Bill Clinton's defining characteristic was pragmatic centrism: triangulation between left and right, welfare reform, deficit reduction, NAFTA — a Democrat who governed from the center. He frustrated liberals and co-opted conservative issues, winning reelection as the man who occupied the middle. Clinton's presidency was the triumph of the vital center.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Clinton repeatedly broke with traditional Democratic values — that was the point of triangulation.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Pragmatic, centrist policy making defined the Clinton presidency.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Clinton kept his distance from party liberals, not a close alliance.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Clinton's relationship with unions was strained, not an unprecedented partnership.

items.stem: The Obama foreign-policy initiative Trump vowed to overturn was
options: A. The Affordable Care Act
B. Border wall construction
C. The Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA)
D. The USA Patriot Act
items.explanation: The Iran nuclear deal — the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (2015) — was Obama's signature foreign-policy initiative, trading sanctions relief for limits on Iran's nuclear program. Donald Trump vowed to overturn it throughout his campaign and withdrew the United States from the deal in 2018. It was the Obama initiative Trump most defined himself against.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Affordable Care Act was domestic policy, not foreign policy.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Border wall construction was Trump's own project, not Obama's.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) was the Obama initiative Trump vowed to overturn.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Patriot Act was Bush-era legislation, not Obama's initiative.

section_1b.directions: Section I, Part B — Short Answer: 3 questions, 40 minutes. Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (A, B, C); write your answers in complete sentences. Question 1 is based on a secondary source, Question 2 on a primary source, and Question 3 on a non-text source (map, chart, image, or diagram). This part counts for 20 percent of the exam score.

questions.stimulus_text: Historian Joseph Ellis writes that the early republic was 'an extended argument about what the Revolution had actually meant' — with the Constitution's silences over federal versus state power guaranteeing that every crisis became a constitutional debate.
parts: A. Briefly explain ONE example of debate over constitutional principles in the United States in the period 1787–1800.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND example of such debate in the same period.
C. Briefly explain ONE example of a political leader acting on constitutional principle in this period.
exemplar: At the 1787 Constitutional Convention, delegates clashed over representation: large states wanted proportional representation while small states demanded equality. The Great Compromise created a Senate with two senators per state and a House apportioned by population.
In 1798 Jefferson and Madison protested the Alien and Sedition Acts with the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, arguing that states could refuse to enforce federal laws they deemed unconstitutional.
President Jefferson justified the Louisiana Purchase on practical rather than strict-constructionist grounds, setting aside his constitutional doubts to double the nation's size.

questions.stimulus_text: For having, upon specious pretenses of public works, raised great unjust taxes upon the commonalty for the advancement of private favorites... and for having protected, favored, and emboldened the Indians against his Majesty's loyal subjects.
questions.attribution: Nathaniel Bacon, 'The Declaration of the People,' July 30, 1676.
parts: A. Briefly describe Bacon's complaint against Governor Berkeley's government in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE development that led frontier Virginians to support Bacon's rebellion.
C. Briefly explain ONE longer-term effect of Bacon's Rebellion on Virginia society.
exemplar: Bacon charges that Berkeley's government taxed ordinary Virginians heavily on false pretenses, using public money to enrich the governor's favorites rather than to serve the colony.

Berkeley's refusal to authorize action against Native peoples - while maintaining a fur-trade monopoly that profited his allies - drove frontier settlers to follow Bacon in armed rebellion against the colonial government.

The rebellion alarmed Virginia's elite into reforms that hardened racial slavery: laws in the following decades stripped rights from free Black people and drew a sharp legal line between white servants and enslaved Africans.

questions.stimulus_text: The photograph shows a West German man using a hammer and chisel to chip a souvenir piece from the Berlin Wall at Potsdamer Platz in November 1989; a large section of the Wall behind him has already been demolished. The image captures ordinary citizens physically dismantling the Cold War's most potent symbol.
questions.attribution: Described from the November 1989 DPLA/U.S. National Archives photograph of the Berlin Wall demolition at Potsdamer Platz (Wikimedia Commons).
parts: A. Briefly describe what the photograph conveys about the end of the Cold War in Europe.
B. Briefly explain ONE development that contributed to the events shown in the photograph.
C. Briefly explain ONE consequence of these events for the role of the United States in the world.
exemplar: The photograph conveys that the Cold War's division of Europe collapsed from below: ordinary people, not diplomats, physically dismantling the wall that symbolized Soviet domination of the East.
Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost and perestroika) and his refusal to use Soviet force to hold the Eastern bloc together allowed East Germans to push through the border in November 1989.

The Cold War's end left the United States as the world's sole superpower, encouraging American-led interventions such as the Gulf War (1991) and debates over whether the U.S. should act as the world's policeman.

section_2a.directions: Section II, Part A — Document-Based Question: 1 question, 60 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period). The question is based on 7 documents. In your response you must develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, use at least 4 documents to support your argument, use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents, and for at least 2 documents explain how the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to your argument. This part counts for 25 percent of the exam score.

dbq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which slavery challenged American national unity in the period from 1844 to 1861.

documents.text: Why, were other reasoning wanting, in favor of now elevating this question of the reception of Texas into the Union, out of the lower region of our past party dissension, up to its proper level of a high and broad nationality, it surely is to be found, found abundantly, in the manner in which other nations have undertaken to intrude themselves into it, between us and the proper parties to the case, in a spirit of hostile interference against us, for the avowed object of thwarting our policy and hampering our power, limiting our greatness and checking the fulfillment of our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions.
documents.sourcing_note: Source: 'Annexation,' by John L. O'Sullivan, United States Magazine and Democratic Review. POV: Democratic editor and expansionist. Purpose: promote Texas annexation under the banner of manifest destiny. Audience: magazine readers. Argument relevance: shows expansionism entangled with slavery from the start - annexing slaveholding Texas forced the slavery-extension question into national politics.

documents.text: As war exists, and notwithstanding all our efforts to avoid it, exists by the act of Mexico herself, we are called upon by every consideration of duty and patriotism to vindicate with decision the honor, rights and dignity of this country.
documents.sourcing_note: Source: President James K. Polk's War Message to Congress. POV: expansionist president. Purpose: justify war with Mexico. Audience: Congress. Argument relevance: the war for territory produced the lands over which the slavery-extension fight would split the nation.

documents.text:
But, sir, the issue now presented is not whether slavery shall exist unmolested where it now is, but whether it shall be carried to new and distant regions, now free, where the footprint of a slave cannot be found. This, sir, is the issue. Upon it I take my stand, and from it I cannot be frightened or driven by idle charges of abolitionism.

I ask not that slavery be abolished, I demand that this government preserve the integrity of free territory against the aggressions of slavery - against its wrongful usurpations.

Sir, I was in favor of the annexation of Texas.... Yes, sir, here was an empire larger than France given up to slavery. Shall further concessions be made by the North? Shall we give up free territory, the inheritance of free labor? Must we yield this also?

...Now, sir, we are told that California is ours, that New Mexico is ours - won by the valor of our arms. They are free. Shall they remain free? Shall these fair provinces be the inheritance and homes of the white labor of freemen or the black labor of slaves? This, sir, is the issue.
documents.sourcing_note: Source: Representative David Wilmot, from the Congressional Globe. POV: Northern Democrat. Purpose: bar slavery from territories won in the Mexican War. Audience: House of Representatives. Argument relevance: shows slavery extension splitting even the Democratic Party along sectional lines - direct evidence of slavery challenging national unity.

documents.text: Described from Reynolds's Political Map of the United States (1856). The map distinguishes free states and territories (light) from slave states (dark), and shows the territories created under the Kansas-Nebraska Act - Nebraska Territory spanning the northern plains, with an 'Indian Reserve' west of Missouri and Arkansas - visualizing how the Act repealed the Missouri Compromise line.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: textbook cartographer. Purpose: illustrate the reach of popular sovereignty. Audience: students. Argument relevance: visualizes how the Kansas-Nebraska Act repealed the Missouri Compromise line, nationalizing the slavery conflict - the map itself shows a nation geographically divided by the issue.
documents.caption: Reynolds's Political Map of the United States, 1856: free states and territories vs. slave states, with the Kansas-Nebraska territorial scheme
documents.pd_rationale: Published 1856 (Wm. C. Reynolds & J. C. Jones; Library of Congress Geography and Map Division scan); license PD-old on Commons (pre-1930 publication; verified in file-page wikitext)

documents.text: The right of property in a slave is distinctly and expressly affirmed in the Constitution.... No word can be found in the Constitution which gives Congress a greater power over the slave property or which entitles property of that kind to less protection than property of any other description.
documents.sourcing_note: Source: Chief Justice Roger Taney, Supreme Court opinion in Dred Scott v. Sandford. POV: pro-southern Chief Justice. Purpose: settle the slavery question judicially by nationalizing slave property rights. Audience: the nation. Argument relevance: instead of settling the issue, the decision outraged the North and deepened sectional disunity.

documents.text: Described from a map of railroads operating in the United States in 1860 (first published 1917). Rail lines form a dense network across the Northeast and Old Northwest, linking the Atlantic seaboard to Chicago and the upper Mississippi, while the South has far fewer and shorter lines.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: economic geography. Purpose: show railroad infrastructure on the eve of the Civil War. Audience: students of transportation history. Argument relevance: the North's dense rail integration versus southern stagnation shows the material base of sectional divergence over slavery's expansion.
documents.caption: Railroads operating in the United States in 1860 (map first published 1917)
documents.pd_rationale: Map first published 1917 in B. H. Meyer's History of Transportation in the United States before 1860 (map by Caroline E. MacGill and collaborators); license PD-US-expired on Commons (pre-1930 publication; verified in file-page wikitext)

documents.text: Described from the 1860 political cartoon 'Progressive Democracy - Prospect of a Smash Up' (National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution). A locomotive labeled 'Equal Rights' carrying Lincoln and Hamlin bears down on a wagon labeled 'Democratic Platform,' pulled in opposite directions by mules carrying the rival Democratic nominations of Douglas and Johnson versus Breckinridge and Lane. Speech bubbles warn of the coming collision.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: Republican-leaning press. Purpose: satirize the Democrats' sectional split in the 1860 election. Audience: voters. Argument relevance: visual proof that slavery shattered the national party system on the eve of secession - the Democracy literally pulling apart.
documents.caption: Currier & Ives, 'Progressive Democracy - Prospect of a Smash Up,' 1860 (Library of Congress)
documents.pd_rationale: 1860 Currier & Ives lithograph (Library of Congress scan); license PD-old-100-1923 on Commons (verified in file-page wikitext)
